title: Regulations and National and International Organizations in Midwifery Practice
introduction: Professional regulation brings order, consistency, and public safety to nursing and midwifery practice. In Nigeria, the statutory mandate rests with the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN), operating alongside global and regional partners including the ICM, UKCC/NMC, WHO, UNICEF, and the West African College of Nursing (WACN).
learningOutcomes: 3.1 Trace the origins of modern nursing regulation and explain the legal establishment, objectives, and 16 statutory functions of the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN).
3.2 Describe the NMCN's organizational structure, 19-member Governing Board, four major departments, seven standing committees, and midwives' legal coverage.
3.3 Explain the purpose and global roles of the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) and the UK regulatory body (UKCC/NMC).
3.4 Compare the structure and maternal-child health roles of the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF.
3.5 Describe the inauguration, objectives, and functions of the West African College of Nursing (WACN) and supporting agencies (UNEP, UNDP, USAID, and Pathfinder).

content.heading: Origin and Legal Establishment of the NMCN
content.body: Modern scientific nursing began with Florence Nightingale (1820-1910) during and after the Crimean War (1854-1856), uniting Christian ideals, discipline, and mission. Nursing was the first health profession to create an international body—the International Council of Nurses (ICN) in 1899—followed by the Royal College of Nursing (1916) and the General Nursing Council for England and Wales (1919). In Nigeria, missionary care, the 1914 amalgamation, and both World Wars accelerated professional growth. On 28th September 1979, the Federal Military Government established the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) via Decree No. 89 of 1979—now codified as the Nursing and Midwifery (Registration, etc.) Act, Cap. N143, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004. The NMCN is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal that can sue and be sued; following a 2001 Presidential management review, it was upgraded from a Category C to a Category B parastatal of the Federal Ministry of Health. Its headquarters are in Abuja, with six Zonal Offices in Sokoto, Kaduna, Bauchi, Enugu, Port Harcourt, and Lagos.

content.heading: Primary Objectives, Statutory Functions, and Collaborations of the NMCN
content.body: The NMCN's three primary objectives are to ensure high-quality nursing and midwifery education in Nigeria, maintain high standards of professional practice, and enforce discipline within the profession. Its 16 specific statutory functions are: (1) indexing all categories of nursing and midwifery students upon starting training; (2) developing and periodically reviewing curricula; (3) cooperating with recognized bodies (NUC, WHO) on new basic and post-basic educational schemes; (4) accrediting all training institutions and clinical practice areas; (5) conducting professional examinations; (6) establishing and maintaining registers of qualified practitioners; (7) conducting registration interviews for foreign-trained nurses and midwives; (8) issuing and renewing Professional Practising Licences every three years; (9) issuing Professional Certificates upon graduation; (10) revoking and/or restoring certificates as applicable; (11) determining and maintaining competency standards; (12) organizing Mandatory Continuing Professional and Educational Development Programmes (MCPDP); (13) conducting and promoting research; (14) maintaining professional discipline via the Nurses and Midwives Tribunal; (15) prosecuting illegal training institutions; and (16) regulating and controlling nursing and midwifery practice in all ramifications. The Council collaborates closely with sister regulatory bodies (Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria, Pharmacists Council of Nigeria), education regulators (NUC, NBTE, JAMB), and national/international NGOs (WHO, UNICEF, USAID, British Council, ICN, ICM, WAHO, IHVN, ICAP, IPAS, FHI, NACA, Pathfinder, and SFH).

content.heading: NMCN Structure, Governing Board, Committees, and Midwives' Legal Coverage
content.body: Policy is formulated by a 19-member Governing Board appointed by the Federal Government on the Federal Ministry of Health's recommendation: (1) Chairman appointed by the Honourable Minister of Health; (2) Head of Nursing Services at the Federal Ministry of Health; (3) four State Heads of Nursing Services rotating across the four health zones; (4) four Educators (Nursing, Midwifery, Public Health, and Psychiatric Nursing) rotating across the four health zones; (5) two representatives of the National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives (NANNM); (6) two Public Interest representatives; (7) two representatives of Universities offering Nursing Degree programmes; (8) one Registered Medical Practitioner (Obstetrician and Gynaecologist); and (9) the Secretary-General/Registrar as Secretary to the Board. The Secretary-General/Registrar serves as Chief Executive and Accounting Officer, supported by four Directors heading the Council's major departments (Education; Inspectorate; Planning, Research and Statistics; and Human Resources, Finance and Accounts) and ~203 staff. Deliberations flow through seven Standing Committees: Education; Examination; Registration; Finance and General Purposes; Standards and Accreditation; Appointment, Promotion and Disciplinary; and the Nurses and Midwives Disciplinary Tribunal. Legally, ignorance is no defence in law: every practising midwife must be registered and licensed under Decree No. 89 of 1979, whose Section 1(1) empowers the Council to determine who are nurses and midwives and what standards of knowledge and skill they must attain.

content.heading: International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) and UKCC (Now NMC)
content.body: According to the International Confederation of Midwives (1996), professional regulation is the means by which order, consistency, and control are brought to a profession and its practice. Founded in 1919 as the International Midwives Union and accredited by the United Nations in 1960, the ICM is a London-based NGO representing over 75 member associations across roughly 66 countries. Working with WHO and FIGO, the ICM helped formulate the international definition of the midwife. Its roles include campaigning for stronger, better-educated, properly regulated midwifery, coordinating the annual International Day of the Midwife, uniting national associations under shared themes, and hosting workshops, seminars, and Triennial Congresses—notably the 1990 Kobe, Japan congress ('Midwifery Education for Safe Motherhood'), whose pre-congress workshop produced the WHO (1996) Safe Motherhood modules recommending strengthened, community-based curricula incorporating selected obstetric emergencies. In the United Kingdom, statutory regulation transferred on 1st July 1983 to the United Kingdom Central Council for Nursing, Midwifery and Health Visiting (UKCC, now the Nursing and Midwifery Council—NMC). Its roles are maintaining the professional register, setting education/practice/conduct standards, advising practitioners, investigating misconduct or unfitness due to ill health, and publishing 'The Scope of Professional Practice' (1992a) to protect the public, protect professional titles, confer accountability and status, and ensure quality care.

content.heading: World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF
content.body: Founded in 1947 with headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland (154 member states noted in the manual), the World Health Organization (WHO) operates through regional offices including AFRO (Brazzaville, Congo), AMRO (Washington, D.C., USA), EURO (Copenhagen, Denmark), SEARO (New Delhi, India), and WPRO (Manila, Philippines). In maternal and child health, WHO launched the 1996 midwifery education modules for safe motherhood, funds midwifery workshops and research, produced the 1994 Mother-Baby Package (recognizing community-based midwives as key to safe motherhood and emphasizing immediate management of haemorrhage, prolonged/obstructed labour, puerperal sepsis, and pregnancy hypertension), publishes technical guidance via the World Health Bulletin, sponsors MCH workforce training, plans Expanded Programmes on Immunization (EPI), and partners with ICM and FIGO. UNICEF (formerly United Nations Children's Emergency Fund, now United Nations Children's Fund) is funded almost entirely by voluntary government, foundation, and public contributions to advance child welfare in developing nations. Its roles include accelerating immunization programmes, sponsoring child-welfare workshops, running electronic media and poster awareness campaigns, promoting child survival (growth monitoring, oral rehydration, breastfeeding, immunization, and family planning), and supporting female literacy and supplementary feeding.

content.heading: West African College of Nursing (WACN) and Supporting Agencies
content.body: The West African College of Nursing (WACN) was inaugurated in April 1981 in Banjul, Gambia as a specialized agency of the West African Health Community (WAHC) to advance basic and post-basic nursing and midwifery education and maintain regional practice standards. WACN's seven core roles are: (1) sponsoring in-service educational programmes, (2) assisting in providing educational facilities, (3) encouraging and promoting nursing/midwifery research, (4) producing textbooks and journals on current practice issues, (5) disbursing research funds to member states, (6) supporting the formation, management, and funding of accredited educational programmes in member states, and (7) organizing workshops and seminars for professional knowledge exchange. Additional supporting international organizations include UNEP (United Nations Environment Programme, handling environmental matters), UNDP (United Nations Development Programme, coordinating UN development activities), USAID (providing funds and commodities for operational research), and Pathfinder (sponsoring family planning commodities and education programmes).

inTextQuestions.question: On what exact date and under which decree was the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) established?
inTextQuestions.answer: On 28th September 1979 by Decree No. 89 of 1979 (now Nursing and Midwifery [Registration, etc.] Act, Cap. N143, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004).

inTextQuestions.question: How often does the NMCN renew Professional Practising Licences for qualified nurses and midwives?
What major maternal health initiative originated at the 1990 ICM Triennial Congress pre-congress workshop in Kobe, Japan?
inTextQuestions.answer: The Safe Motherhood midwifery education modules (launched by WHO in 1996), recommending stronger community-based midwifery curricula and training in managing selected obstetric emergencies.

inTextQuestions.question: When and where was the West African College of Nursing (WACN) inaugurated?
inTextQuestions.answer: In April 1981 in Banjul, Gambia, as a specialized agency of the West African Health Community (WAHC).

saqs.question: State the three primary objectives of the NMCN and list six of its specific statutory functions.
saqs.answer: Its three primary objectives are ensuring high-quality nursing and midwifery education, maintaining high standards of professional practice, and enforcing discipline within the profession. Six statutory functions include: (1) indexing students on commencement of training, (2) developing and reviewing curricula, (3) accrediting training schools and clinical sites, (4) conducting professional examinations and maintaining registers, (5) issuing certificates and 3-yearly practising licences (and revoking/restoring them), and (6) maintaining discipline through the Nurses and Midwives Tribunal and prosecuting illegal schools.

saqs.question: Describe the composition of the 19-member NMCN Governing Board and list its seven Standing Committees.
saqs.answer: The 19-member Board comprises the Chairman (appointed by Minister of Health), Head of Nursing Services (FMOH), 4 State Heads of Nursing Services (rotating across 4 zones), 4 Educators (Nursing, Midwifery, Public Health, Psychiatric—rotating), 2 NANNM reps, 2 Public Interest reps, 2 University Nursing reps, 1 Obstetrician/Gynaecologist, and the Secretary-General/Registrar. Its seven Standing Committees are: Education, Examination, Registration, Finance and General Purposes, Standards and Accreditation, Appointment/Promotion/Disciplinary, and the Nurses and Midwives Disciplinary Tribunal.

saqs.question: Explain the roles of the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) and the UKCC (now NMC) in regulating and strengthening midwifery.
saqs.answer: ICM (founded 1919, London office) unites over 75 associations across ~66 countries to campaign for stronger midwifery education and regulation, coordinates the annual International Day of the Midwife, hosts Triennial Congresses and workshops (e.g., 1990 Kobe Safe Motherhood workshop), and co-authored the international midwife definition with WHO and FIGO. UKCC/NMC (statutory control from 1st July 1983) maintains the UK register, sets education/conduct standards, advises practitioners, investigates misconduct/unfitness, and protects the public and professional title.

saqs.question: Compare the maternal and child health roles of WHO and UNICEF, naming the African Regional Office of WHO.
saqs.answer: WHO (founded 1947, Geneva HQ; AFRO in Brazzaville, Congo) launched the 1996 Safe Motherhood midwifery modules and 1994 Mother-Baby Package, strengthens community midwifery skills for obstetric emergencies (haemorrhage, obstructed labour, puerperal sepsis, hypertension), publishes the World Health Bulletin, funds training/research, and plans EPI. UNICEF (voluntarily funded) accelerates immunization, sponsors child-welfare workshops and media awareness, promotes growth monitoring, oral rehydration, breastfeeding, immunization, and family planning, and funds female literacy and supplementary feeding.

saqs.question: Outline five roles of the West African College of Nursing (WACN) and briefly state the focus of USAID and Pathfinder.
saqs.answer: Five WACN roles are: sponsoring in-service programmes, providing educational facilities, promoting research and disbursing research funds, producing nursing/midwifery textbooks and journals, and supporting accredited educational programmes and workshops across member states. USAID provides funds and commodities for operational research, while Pathfinder sponsors family planning commodities and education programmes.
